_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: But with two sets: for example, he set aside two piles of money as a guarantee and achieved atonement with one, so that the other is pushed aside; one might say that he [Rabbi Shimon] does not hold [that it goes to gift offerings].
rashi:a1.2: It teaches us: [that is,] Rabbi Ami [teaches us].
gershom:a1.1: But with two sets: that is, two piles, and one of them is left over; he [Rabbi Shimon] does not hold [that it goes to gift offerings].
gershom:a2.1: It teaches us: Rabbi Ami, who holds [that even Rabbi Shimon allows it].
gershom:a3.1: One who designates as a guarantee, is it necessary [to say] that it grazes? For here there is no lost animal at all.
rashi:a4.1: Five sin offerings die: in every circumstance in which they occur; and this is one of them, [a sin offering] whose owner has achieved atonement.
gershom:a4.1: Rather, according to Rabbi Shimon? But he said that five sin offerings die, and one of them is a sin offering whose owner has achieved atonement. And here one cannot say: but Rabbi Shimon does hold [that surplus goes to] gift offerings! For we said that when he holds so, that applies only to the surplus money of a sin offering; but here, where the sin offering itself is left over, according to Rabbi Shimon it certainly dies.
gershom:a5.1: Rather, according to Rabbi: he says it grazes; for when Rabbi said “it dies,” that was with a lost animal, but with a guarantee, the one that is left over grazes.
rashi:a7.1: He holds like Rabbi: who said that one lost at the time of designation dies, because its owner achieved atonement [with another]. And when one designates a second as a guarantee, the owner will also achieve atonement with another, and it dies. This version is straightforward.
rashi:a7.2: He holds like Rabbi: who is stringent and says that one who designates [a replacement] for a lost animal, it is considered as lost. And learn from it that even where there is no loss, as here, where the first was not lost but [the second stood] as a guarantee, for when the first became blemished he designated that one in this way, and even so it dies.
gershom:a8.1: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon says: If the second, which he brought with its money, was sacrificed before the first was slaughtered, it dies, even though it has gone out to non-sacred status. “It enters your mind that Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon holds like Rabbi”: and why does it say “it enters your mind that he holds like Rabbi”? Because Rabbi Oshaya spoke according to Rabbi, and it wants to challenge him from Rabbi, who said that one of them is sacrificed and the second dies. Just as Rabbi holds so for one who designated his sin offering and it was lost, so too Rabbi holds even [for one who designates them as a guarantee; the edition corrects the text to read so], since the owner has already achieved atonement. And since even in this case, where it is non-sacred, Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon says that the first dies, all the more so [even with a guarantee], where one designated two sin offerings as a guarantee and both bear the name of a sin offering: if he achieved atonement with one, its partner dies. And this is difficult for Rabbi Oshaya.
gershom:a10.1: Another version: but here one cannot say “it is a mitzva with the first, and that is why the second dies”; rather, here even the first dies. Apparently monetary sanctity is strong, for this blemished animal, which has only monetary sanctity, is rejected, and even though it was redeemed it dies. Is it not that even Rabbi, who said “and the second dies,” holds that in this case it dies, and all the more so [it would die] with a guarantee?
rashi:a8.1: He holds like his father, who said five sin offerings die: in every circumstance in which they occur.
gershom:a9.1: He [Rabbi Oshaya] can say to you: No, perhaps Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon holds like his father, who said five sin offerings die, etc., and a sin offering whose owner achieved atonement is [among them]; and I did not speak according to Rabbi Shimon but according to Rabbi.
gershom:a11.1: He does not hold like Rabbi in this; rather, Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon holds like his father, as we said.
rashi:a9.1: Because a communal sin offering does not die: this refers to the goats of Yom Kippur.
rashi:a10.1: Living animals are not rejected: and the first [goat] is not rejected by the death of its partner. And when he achieves atonement, if he wishes, he may achieve atonement with the second of the first pair; and the other one, the latter, is like one he designated as a guarantee, that is, it was not designated in place of a lost one, since from the first pair only the goat for Azazel died, not the one for the Name. And even so it dies, and this is difficult for Rabbi Oshaya [the daf: Rabbi Hoshaya].
tosafot:a10.1: And the other is a guarantee, and it teaches that an individual’s dies: And if you say: above, the Gemara challenged Rabbi Abba from this very case, treating it as one who designates for a lost animal, while here it treats it as one who designates as a guarantee? One can say: now it understands that since, at the time he designated the second, he knew that he would achieve atonement not with it but with the second of the first pair, it is a guarantee. It is unlike the designation for a lost animal above, for there he thought the first was lost and that he would achieve atonement with the one he was now designating, so it was like designating for a lost animal and not a guarantee. But here, since he knew at the time he designated the second that he would achieve atonement with the first, it is like a guarantee; and even so it says that an individual’s dies. And this is difficult for Rabbi Oshaya, who said that one who designates two sin offerings as a guarantee achieves atonement with one of them and the second grazes. And it answers: Rav conforms to his reasoning, as he said it is a mitzva with the first, so from the moment it was designated it was designated for loss, and this is not a guarantee, and therefore it dies. And what [the Gemara] compared it to above, to one who designates for a lost animal, was for the reason that the mitzva is with the first. Or perhaps one can explain that here it holds like Rav Huna, who said above that if it is not lost it does not die, neither according to Rabbi nor according to the Rabbis; and that is why it challenged from it, since it thought it was like one who designates as a guarantee.
gershom:a6.1: And the other, the second of the second pair, is a guarantee: for if the second of the first pair is lost, this one is sacrificed in its stead; and it teaches that an individual’s dies. This is difficult for Rabbi Oshaya, who said its partner grazes. Rabbi Oshaya can say to you: Rav says living animals are not rejected, and when he achieves atonement, etc. He [Rav] holds like Rabbi Yosei, who said with regard to the Paschal offering that it is a mitzva with the first. Here too it is a mitzva with the first, and so the other, the second of the second pair, was designated for loss, and anything designated for loss is considered as lost.
rashi:a11.1: Rav holds like Rabbi Yosei, who said it is a mitzva with the first, as is taught about Paschal offerings: One designated his Paschal offering and it was lost, and he designated another in its stead, and then the first was found; he may sacrifice whichever he wishes. Rabbi Yosei says: it is a mitzva with the first. And Rav holds like him. And since it is a mitzva with the first, it is like one who designates for a lost animal: the second was designated at the outset not for the sake of consecration but so that it would be lost and go to its death, since he holds it is a mitzva with the first. But with two sin offerings as a guarantee, since if he wished he could achieve atonement with this one, which is fitting, one cannot say that it was designated at the outset for loss.
gershom:a7.1: [Continuing Rabbi Oshaya’s answer:] And where did Rabbi say “it dies”? With a lost animal; but with a guarantee, where there is no lost animal, Rabbi did not say so. Therefore this ruling, that an individual’s dies, follows Rabbi Yosei, and I do not hold so.
rashi:a16.1: One may not flay a firstborn from its feet: the way one begins to strip the hide by way of the legs and turns it inside out whole, for the needs of smiths [for bellows] or for honey; as opposed to one who does not want to strip it whole, who strips it with a knife along its belly, from its throat to its tail.
rashi:a16.2: Nor with disqualified consecrated animals: that were redeemed and he slaughtered them.
gershom:a12.1: One may not flay from the feet: on a Festival, stripping the hide of an animal whole for the needs of a bellows. It is called margilin because for that purpose one begins stripping the hide by way of the legs [raglayim]. And on a Festival it is prohibited, since one exerts excessive effort.
rashi:a18.1: An Israelite may not be counted with the priest: to eat with the priest the meat of a blemished firstborn that a priest slaughtered. Apparently, even though it became blemished, it retains its sanctity; therefore one may not flay it from the feet, since that resembles labor with sacred animals and the practices of non-sacred ones.
rashi:a19.1: The blemished one shall be redeemed: before the designation of the second. And these two sin offerings were designated for a single sin: a blemish befell the first and he designated the second in its stead.
rashi:a20.1: The blemished one was slaughtered: after its redemption.
rashi:a20.2: Prohibited: since it is a sin offering whose owner achieved atonement.
rashi:a21.1: Goes out to the place of burning: the meat of the blemished one. Apparently, even though it was redeemed and slaughtered, it retains its sanctity and is called a sin offering whose owner achieved atonement. Therefore, with regard to flaying from the feet too, even though it was redeemed and slaughtered, it retains its sanctity.
tosafot:a21.1: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon says: even the meat of the blemished one in the pot, etc.: And if you say: how is this different from our mishna [22b]? There the Rabbis say that even if the blood of the second was sprinkled while the first, the blemished one, still exists, it is not subject to death; yet here it says that if the blemished one was slaughtered after the blood of the unblemished one was sprinkled, it is prohibited, and according to Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon, even if the meat is in the pot when the blood of the unblemished one is sprinkled, it goes out to the place of burning; while in the mishna he says that if the blemished one was slaughtered before the sprinkling of the unblemished one’s blood, it is fit. One can distinguish: in the case of the mishna, since it was already blemished before the other was designated, it does not carry so much sanctity; but here, where they were designated as a guarantee and both appeared fit to be sacrificed, it carries more sanctity.
gershom:a13.1: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon says: even if the blemished one was slaughtered before the sprinkling of the unblemished one’s blood, and the meat of the blemished one is in the pot, and the blood of the unblemished one was sprinkled before the meat of the blemished one was eaten, it goes out to the place of burning. Apparently, according to Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon, even though he slaughtered the blemished one, which is [one of the] disqualified consecrated animals, it retains its sanctity though it was redeemed: if the blood of the unblemished one was sprinkled before it was eaten, it goes out to the place of burning.
rashi:a22.1: Both as Beit Shammai: for surely, just as Beit Shammai are stringent with a firstborn, they are also stringent with other disqualified consecrated animals. Why did he establish the first clause as Beit Shammai and the latter clause as Rabbi [Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon]?
gershom:a14.1: And let him establish both: the firstborn and the disqualified consecrated animals, as Beit Shammai; and say that just as they hold for a firstborn that even though he slaughtered it, it retains its sanctity and one does not treat it with disgrace by flaying it from the feet, so too they hold for disqualified consecrated animals.
rashi:a25.1: A firstborn has no redemption, as it is written: “You shall not redeem” (Numbers 18:17); and if one redeemed it, its redemption money does not take on its sanctity.
gershom:a15.1: Perhaps Beit Shammai said so only, etc. [The comment then gives the reasoning of the Gemara’s answer about Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon:] only with disqualified consecrated animals, which are strong enough to take hold of their redemption, for their sanctity [passes] onto its redemption and they go out to non-sacred status; but not a firstborn, of which it is written: “You shall not redeem.”
rashi:a26.1: Slaughtered in the butchers’ market: apparently they do not retain their sanctity once they have been redeemed and slaughtered.
rashi:a26.2: Apparently, since you permitted him: to sell it in the market, he adds and redeems it from the Temple treasury at a high price, since in the end he will sell it well. With flaying from the feet too, let him be permitted to flay; for since he knows at the time he redeems the disqualified consecrated animal that in the end he will flay it and sell the hide for a higher price, he will add and redeem it from the Temple treasury.
gershom:a16.1: And does Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon not hold that all disqualified consecrated animals are sold in the butchers’ market, which treats them with disgrace by selling them in the market? What is the reason [it is permitted]? Since you permitted him to treat them as he wishes, to weigh them and sell them in the market, he adds and redeems it at a high price. Here too, since you permitted him to flay it from the feet, he adds and redeems them at a high price.
rashi:a27.1: What improves the hide damages the meat: what he gains in the price of the hide he loses in the price of the meat, and there is no profit here; for since he is afraid to cut the hide, he cuts the meat, and then it is no longer nice to sell.
gershom:a17.1: Rav Mari said: [This is why] Rabbi Elazar does not hold this. What is the reason? What improves the hide damages the meat; therefore he does not hold it.
rashi:a28.1: Because it appears like one who performs labor with sacred animals: for he makes a bellows out of the animal while it is still whole. Actual labor it certainly is not, for there is no labor after death; but it looks like labor.
gershom:a18.1: In the West they said: it is prohibited for this reason, that it looks like one who performs labor with sacred animals.
rashi:a29.1: A decree lest he raise from them: from disqualified consecrated animals.
rashi:a29.2: Many flocks: for if you permit him to flay from the feet, he will keep them and not slaughter them until bellows-makers happen by, and he will come to raise flocks, and come to the stumbling block of shearing and work; and disqualified consecrated animals are prohibited for shearing and work even after their redemption.
gershom:a19.1: And Rabbi Yosei bar Avin said: he prohibited it for this reason: if you permit flaying from the feet, sometimes the bellows-makers, who buy hides for bellows, are not to be found there, and people would keep the animals and raise flocks from them. It is a decree lest they come to a stumbling block with them and work them. Therefore they decreed that one may not flay disqualified consecrated animals from the feet, so that people will not come to keep them.
gershom:a20.1: Hadran alakh Vlad Ḥatat: we will return to you, “The Offspring of a Sin Offering.”
rashi:b1.1: Mishna. Employ artifice: to take it away from the priest and set it aside for his own obligation.
rashi:b1.2: If it gave birth to a male, it shall be sacrificed as a burnt offering: for a firstborn becomes sacred only at [the opening of] the womb, and since he enclosed it in a different sanctity beforehand, the sanctity of a firstborn no longer takes effect.
rashi:b1.3: And if: he said, “If it gives birth to a female, let it be a peace offering”; if it gave birth to a female, it is sacrificed as a peace offering.
rashi:b2.1: If it gave birth to two males: the sanctity of a burnt offering takes effect on both of them, since he said “If male, let it be a burnt offering”; but he vowed only one. Therefore he sacrifices one for his vow, and the second is sold for the needs of a burnt offering, and its money is non-sacred.
rashi:b4.1: Gemara. A burnt offering, yes: since it is burned entirely, one is permitted to change the firstborn’s sanctity to its sanctity; but peace offerings, which are of lesser sanctity, one may not change the firstborn’s sanctity to theirs ab initio; and all the more so it is prohibited to inflict a blemish on it, which takes it out of its sanctity entirely.
rashi:b6.1: Lest most of its head emerge: and the womb sanctifies it, and then he inflicts a blemish on it, and it is inflicting a blemish on sacred animals. It teaches us that we do not decree, for he will take care to inflict the blemish once a little has emerged, before most of its head emerges, as we say in Bekhorot (35a): a kid by its ears, for the kid emerges by way of its temples and the ears appear first; and a lamb by its lips, for the lamb’s mouth emerges first.
rashi:b7.1: This is preferable: to permit inflicting a blemish on it while it is not yet sanctified, so that the priest will not need to keep it but will hurry to slaughter it. For if he does not inflict a blemish on it, he must keep it until a blemish befalls it, and in the meantime he comes to shearing and work.
rashi:b7.2: Deficient is preferable [Rashi’s text reads ḥasira, “deficient,” where the printed Gemara reads yatira, “much”]: that is, that he removes a limb from it before most of it emerges and makes it a blemished animal.
rashi:b8.1: Is a female sanctified as a firstborn: that one would need to employ artifice regarding it? For it says “How does one employ artifice” and counts this case.
rashi:b8.2: To a consecrated animal: that if it is a sin offering and became pregnant, and he wishes to employ artifice so that [the offspring] will not go to its death, since the offspring of a sin offering goes to its death, he changes it to a different sanctity. And it teaches us that the offspring of sacred animals are sacred upon coming into being and not in their mothers’ womb; and since it is not yet sanctified with its mother’s sanctity, he can impose another sanctity on it, so that when it is born it is not the offspring of a sin offering.
rashi:b8.3: The language of the Jerusalem Talmud: “Is a female, etc.? [It refers] to a mevakeret of consecrated animals,” that is, a consecrated animal, as I explained. And the word mevakeret [one giving birth to its firstborn] is not precise here; but since the first clause taught about a non-sacred mevakeret, it uses the word mevakeret here too.
rashi:b9.1: If it is a consecrated animal: why is the second sold to those obligated to bring a burnt offering? Let the first one that emerges be a burnt offering, and the other, when it is born, should have its mother’s sanctity.
rashi:b9.2: This latter clause: of “it gave birth to two males,” we come back to a non-sacred animal. So the first clause and the latter clause concern non-sacred animals, and the middle one a consecrated animal.
tosafot:b1.1: Mishna: How does one employ artifice. [Only the heading appears here; the comment follows in the next note.]
tosafot:b1.2: If male, a burnt offering: it is explained in the Gemara that it says a burnt offering specifically, which does not lower its sanctity, but not peace offerings, which lower its sanctity. And on “if female, peace offerings,” the Gemara challenges: is a female sanctified as a firstborn? That is, he need not enclose it in a sanctity. And it establishes it with a consecrated animal, where he does not want the mother’s sanctity to take effect on it and wants to enclose it in a different sanctity. And the latter clause, “it gave birth to two males,” it establishes with a non-sacred animal; so the first clause and the latter clause concern non-sacred animals, and the middle clause a consecrated animal. My teacher, the RaMaR, found it difficult: why did it not strain to establish the middle clause with a non-sacred animal too? For the latter clause speaks of non-sacred animals, and even so he enclosed [the female] as peace offerings. And he answered: because it wants to fit it with “How does one employ artifice.”
tosafot:b4.1: Rav Yehuda says: it is permitted to inflict a blemish on a firstborn: as it says in Bekhorot (35a): a kid by its ears, a lamb by its lips. And if you say: let us say that Rav Yehuda here disagrees with Rav Huna in chapter Behema HaMakshah (Ḥullin 69b): if a third emerged and he sold it to a gentile, and then another third emerged, it is sanctified as a firstborn, because when the majority emerged at the end it became clear retroactively that it was sanctified from the outset; here too let us say so for one who inflicts a blemish. One can distinguish between inflicting a blemish and selling: with selling there is more room to err, lest he sell after the majority has emerged.
tosafot:b7.1: This is much preferable to his coming to shearing and work: Explanation: if it has no blemish, he must keep it, and there is reason to fear lest he come to the stumbling block of shearing and work; but now that it has a blemish, the priest slaughters it and does not come to shearing and work, for why would he keep it? And Rabbeinu Tam said: nowadays people are accustomed to sell part of the mother [to a gentile] in order to take the offspring out of firstborn status, and it is good to do so, provided that he transfers it to him with a significant act of acquisition, such as lifting, for a small animal, or pulling, together with an acquisition by money. And although in the first chapter of Bekhorot (3b) [it is told] of Rav Mari bar Raḥel, who would transfer [the ears of his animals] to a gentile, etc., and the animals of Rav Mari bar Raḥel died out; and it is said about that, that they died out because he took them away from the priest, and it is forbidden to do so; or else because Rav Mari knew how to transfer a complete acquisition, while not everyone knows, and they think he performed a mere gesture, and they come to a stumbling block. And we hold like the latter version, that a complete acquisition is required. And even according to the first version, we are more comfortable selling it to a gentile than inflicting a blemish on it before most of it emerges, since then he will not come to err and inflict the blemish after most has emerged. Therefore it is good to do so and sell part of the mother to a gentile before the birth; and this is preferable, for he will not come to the stumbling block of shearing and work.
gershom:b1.1: How does one employ artifice on the firstborn, etc.: for a firstborn is not sanctified until the opening of the womb sanctifies it; but while it is in its mother’s womb, he may change it to something else.
gershom:b2.1: And the second is sold to those obligated to bring burnt offerings, and its money is non-sacred: it is sold to those obligated to bring burnt offerings for this reason. (The edition notes that the text seems to need correcting, to read:) for he said “if male, a burnt offering” without specifying, and it is not known, etc.; that is, if it gave birth to a male, let it be a burnt offering, and moreover it is not known about which one he said it. Therefore the second is sold to those obligated to bring burnt offerings, [and for this reason] its money is non-sacred, for in any case he consecrated only one.
gershom:b3.1: It gave birth to two females: its law is as with two males.
gershom:b4.1: It is permitted to inflict a blemish on a firstborn before it emerges into the air of the world: for example, if its ear or its lip emerged first, and he inflicted a blemish on it before most of its head emerged, it is sacrificed as a burnt offering.
gershom:b5.1: A burnt offering, yes: that is, to the status of a burnt offering, whose sanctity is more stringent than a firstborn’s, he may change it; but peace offerings, whose sanctity is lesser than a firstborn’s, since they are eaten by Israelites, it may not be sacrificed [as such]; and all the more so inflicting a blemish, which makes it non-sacred, is prohibited.
gershom:b6.1: Rav Yehuda holds: the mishna, from which we inferred “as a burnt offering, yes; as peace offerings, no,”
gershom:b7.1: [applies] when the Temple is standing; and when I say it is permitted to inflict a blemish, I say it of the present time.
gershom:b8.1: And say that indeed: that for this reason we should decree that one may not.
gershom:b9.1: Even so, this is preferable: to inflict a blemish on it; for if he does not inflict a blemish on it, perhaps he will come to shearing.
gershom:b10.1: Another version: this is what Rav Yehuda teaches us: that deficient is preferable [Rabbeinu Gershom too reads ḥasira, “deficient,” for the printed yatira], so that he does not come, etc.
gershom:b11.1: If female, peace offerings: why did it need to say this? A female would be non-sacred anyway; is a female sanctified as a firstborn? Rather, the latter clause, which teaches “if it gave birth to an unblemished female, it shall be sacrificed as peace offerings,” teaches about a consecrated animal: if one consecrated a pregnant animal and said, “If it gives birth to a female, let it be peace offerings,” it is peace offerings. He holds that a fetus is not considered a limb of its mother. (The edition sets aside the words “another version, like the first version,” and adds:) [They say: this animal giving birth to its firstborn, what is it? If it is consecrated, why is the second sold? The one he consecrated as a burnt offering, etc.]
gershom:b12.1: The latter clause comes back [the edition notes a gap of about two lines here] to a non-sacred animal. For example, where it is not known about which of the males he said “a burnt offering”; therefore the second is sold for the needs of burnt offerings and its money is non-sacred, as we said above.
gershom:b13.1: Another version: the latter male is merely non-sacred; but since we do not know which emerged first, the second is sold for the needs of a burnt offering and its money is non-sacred, for in any case his intention for a burnt offering was only for one.
